cover.alt: Evening on a Florentine bridge over the Arno in April 1300: two young clerks lean on the parapet in the wind, one talking with his hands, the other listening.
cover.art_brief: Florence, a windy April evening in 1300, on a stone bridge over the Arno (the Ponte Vecchio of the time: a plain stone bridge with a few low wooden shops, no later buildings). Gherardo, sixteen or seventeen, lean, quick, in a travel-stained dark tunic, leans on the parapet and talks with open hands; Lapo, sixteen, dark-haired, in a plain shop tunic with ink on his fingers, listens beside him, half turned away toward the water. Wind in their hair and cloaks; late light on the river and the towers of the city behind. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash, as in the earlier covers. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

inference_aids.alt: Gherardo stands in the doorway of the Cerchi shop without coming in; Lapo faces him from inside, with bales of wool behind him; further in, a partner watches from among the cloth.
inference_aids.art_brief: Late afternoon, April 1300, the doorway of the Cerchi company shop in the sesto of Porta San Piero. Gherardo, sixteen or seventeen, lean, in a dark Spini clerk's tunic, stands exactly on the threshold, not entering, his face tight and unsmiling, one hand on the door frame. Lapo, sixteen, in a plain shop tunic, faces him from just inside, a pen still in his hand. Behind Lapo, stacked bales of wool and folded cloth; further back in the shadowed shop, a middle-aged partner in a good fur-trimmed gown stands among the cloth, watching the door. Old Ser Bindo is a small figure at the counter in the far background, bent over the big book. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
words_with_history.text: Gherardo aveva un'altra voce. A Roma il pane era caro, e i pellegrini pagavano con l'oro.
words_with_history.note_en:
The imperfect keeps the Latin imperfect, with -b- softened to -v-: habebat → aveva, amabat → amava, tacebat → taceva, ridebat → rideva. Essere keeps its own Latin stem: erat → era, erant → erano. Latin eram gave Old Italian io era, as Dante and the old Florentines wrote it (and io avea, io aveva); the modern ero, avevo have an -o added later by analogy with the -o of the first-person present (io canto, io sono). So the modern persons -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano correspond to Latin -bam, -bas, -bat, -bamus, -batis, -bant, but not every ending is a direct sound outcome.

Most Italian nouns continue the Latin accusative, not the nominative, after final -m had disappeared in spoken Latin and the cases had collapsed into one form: pontem → ponte, vocem → voce, panem → pane, partem → parte, pacem → pace (peace), legem → legge (law). This is why an Italian noun so often shows the stem that the Latin nominative hides: pons, vox, pars, pax, lex. Città is civitatem, cut short.

Latin au often became Italian o: aurum → oro, causam → cosa, paucum → poco, pauperem → povero. These are historical developments, not a substitution rule. Auscultare → ascoltare (listen) went another way: its au was reduced to a (Latin had a variant ascultare), and the short u became o. Paura (fear) is not an au word at all: it reshapes Latin pavor with the suffix -ura and then loses the v between vowels, so its vowels stand in separate syllables, pa-u-ra.

Two words to watch: Latin quasi is mostly 'as if', but Italian quasi kept only its other sense, 'nearly, almost' (Latin paene); and sentire is mostly 'hear' (Latin audire), though it keeps the Latin sense 'feel, perceive' too.

grammar.title: Rideva e rise
grammar.rule: Gherardo rideva; poi rise. Ser Bindo scriveva; poi scrisse ancora un numero. «Lo fai per me?» «Non lo faccio.»
grammar.note_en:
**The imperfect against the passato remoto.** Italian's imperfect (aveva, era, rideva) and passato remoto (ebbe, fu, rise) continue the Latin imperfect and perfect, and the difference between them is the one you know. The imperfect describes the background, a state, or what used to happen again and again: «Tutti pagavano» (They all paid, everyone was paying); «Io sedevo alla tavola dalla mattina alla sera» (I sat at the table from morning to evening); Ogni mattina lui contava la lana (Every morning he counted wool). The remoto tells a single event that moves the story on: «Un giorno un cardinale mi chiamò nel suo palazzo» (One day a cardinal summoned me to his palace). Gherardo's Rome story turns on this: weeks of crowds and money in the imperfect, then one day, one cardinal, in the remoto.

The same verb can take either tense in one scene, and the choice says something: Ser Bindo scriveva, e non lo guardò (Ser Bindo was writing, and did not look at him) but Ser Bindo scrisse ancora un numero, poi lasciò la penna (Ser Bindo wrote one more figure, then put down his pen). Gherardo rideva di nuovo (Gherardo was laughing again: his mood that evening), but Poi rise, e guardò l'Arno (Then he laughed, and looked at the Arno). Tessa lo guardava (Tessa was watching him, all through Baldo's talk); Tessa guardò Lapo a lungo (Tessa looked at Lapo for a long time): a remoto can last, but it is one act, seen whole. Cione taceva (Cione said nothing, all through supper); Gherardo lo vide, e tacque (Gherardo saw him, and fell silent). Era quasi sera quando Gherardo venne alla porta della bottega (It was almost evening when Gherardo came to the shop door): the imperfect sets the time, the remoto brings him to the door. In the table Rideva e rise the left column is the imperfect and the right the passato remoto.

Inside reported speech the imperfect keeps describing, and here Italian parts company with Latin: an indirect question or statement stays in the indicative, where Latin would use the subjunctive (qui essent, quid facerent) or the accusative and infinitive. «Poi mi domandò di Firenze, e dei Cerchi: chi erano, che cosa facevano, quanto oro avevano» (Then he asked me about Florence and the Cerchi: who they were, what they did, how much gold they had); «Dissi che erano mercanti di lana» (I said they were wool merchants), not mercatores eos esse.

**Forms of the imperfect.** Remove the infinitive's -re and add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano: conta-re → conta-vo, conta-va (I, he counted); paga-re → paga-vano (they paid); sede-re → sede-vo (I sat); ride-re → ride-va (he laughed); veni-re → veni-vano (they came). Fare and dire use the longer stems face- and dice-, familiar from Latin facere and dicere: facevamo (we did), facevano (they did), dicevo (I kept saying: «Io lo dicevo», I always said so). Essere is irregular: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano. The table Ero, eri, era shows the forms the story uses. Note that voi is also the plain plural 'you': «E voi degli Spini?» (And you Spini men?), «Avevate paura?» (Were you afraid?), Lapo to Gherardo and his fellows.

**The remoto in speech.** Florentines told finished events in the remoto even in conversation, and even of yesterday: «Ieri li condannò» (Yesterday it sentenced them); «Lo vedesti?» (Did you see him?). Much present-day conversation would use the compound past here (chapter 4); usage varies by region, and the remoto remains alive in Tuscan speech. The first and second persons appear in dialogue: dissi (I said, Latin dixi), dicesti (you said, dixisti), vedesti (you saw, vidisti), vedemmo (we saw, vidimus). Recognise them; you will not need to produce them yet.

**Object pronouns lo, la, li, le.** Italian made its object pronouns from ille, as it made its articles: illum → lo (him, it), illam → la (her, it), illos → li (them), illas → le (them, feminine). They stand before a finite verb: «Lo vedesti?» (Did you see him? lo = il papa); «La notizia, in casa Donati, la sanno tutti» (The news, in the Donati house everyone knows it); «Quei tre uomini, io li conosco» (Those three men, I know them). Before a vowel lo and la become l': Lapo l'ascoltava (Lapo was listening to him); «Le parole, tu le senti in bottega, e la sera le porti a me» (The words, you hear them in the shop, and in the evening you bring them to me). With an infinitive the pronoun is attached to the end, and the infinitive loses its final -e: dire + lo = dirlo, sapere + lo = saperlo: «Non posso dirlo» (I can't say it); «Devi saperlo» (You must know it). Lo often stands for a whole statement, as in «Lo so» (I know), «Non lo so» (I don't know), and in the chapter's last turn: «Lo fai per me?» (Will you do it for me?) – «Non lo faccio» (I won't do it). The present here speaks of the future, as in chapter 1. Mi and ti are 'me' and 'you'. In «Un cardinale mi chiamò» (A cardinal summoned me) mi is a direct object; in «Non ti credo» (I don't believe you) ti is indirect, 'to you', as in Latin tibi credo. The forms are the same in both functions.

**Si.** Si guardarono means 'they looked at each other': si here is reciprocal, like Latin inter se.

**Older forms.** Ser Bindo says niuno (= nessuno, nobody); messere or messer (sir, title of knights and judges) and Ser (title of a notary) are the titles of chapter 1.

**Fact and fiction.** On 18 April 1300 Florence convicted three men tied to the Spini company and the papal court (Simone Gherardi, Noffo Quintavalle and Cambio da Sesto) of plotting with Pope Boniface VIII against the commune; the prosecution was led by messer Lapo Saltarelli and two others. Boniface protested in writing on 15 May; Baldo's talk at supper is rumour running ahead of that letter. Boniface had proclaimed the Jubilee on 22 February 1300. Dante, Inferno XVIII 28–33, describes the Jubilee crowds on the bridge to St Peter's kept in two streams, one going toward the church and one coming back, the picture Gherardo gives. Gherardo, the partner, the cardinal and Gherardo's acquaintance with the condemned men are fiction.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Questions 1–2: answer in Italian or English, in your own words, then compare with the model. Questions 3–4 are Dal latino all'italiano, in English or Italian. (3) Write the Italian imperfect from the story for each Latin form, in this order: erat, habebat, tacebat, ridebat. (4) Write the Italian noun from the story for each Latin accusative, in this order: pontem, vocem, panem, partem. Which Latin case do they continue, and what do they show that the nominatives pons, vox, pars hide?

items.prompt: Ser Bindo disse: «I Cerchi non congiurano. Aspettano.» Perché il socio rise?
model_answers: Perché per il socio messer Vieri aspetta sempre: teme il papa, e il papa, che non aspetta, vuole Firenze.
items.rubric: The partner hears Bindo's line as the firm's weakness, not its virtue: Vieri de' Cerchi fears the pope and waits («aspetta tutta la vita»), while the pope does not wait and wants Florence; the Spini hold the pope's gold and he holds them. Any answer that sees the laugh as mockery of Vieri's caution is right. An English answer is fine.

items.prompt: Sul ponte, che cosa domandò Gherardo a Lapo, e che cosa rispose Lapo?
model_answers: Gherardo domandò a Lapo di portare sul ponte le parole dei soci e di Ser Bindo. Lapo rispose: «No. Non lo faccio.»
items.rubric: It is enough to say that Gherardo asked Lapo to bring him the shop's talk (what the partners and Ser Bindo say) on the bridge in the evening, and that Lapo refused («Non lo faccio»). Further details are welcome but not required: the Spini fear the trial; Lapo cannot say why he refuses («Non lo so. Ma non lo faccio.»); they part friends. An English answer is fine.

erat → era (Era quasi sera); habebat → aveva (aveva un'altra voce); tacebat → taceva (Cione ... taceva); ridebat → rideva (non rideva più; rideva di nuovo). These continue Latin third-person singular imperfects in -bat; essere keeps its own stem.

pontem → ponte, vocem → voce, panem → pane, partem → parte. These words continue the Latin accusatives, with final -m lost (it had disappeared in spoken Latin); pontem, vocem and partem show stems that are hidden in the nominatives pons, vox, pars.

provenance.author: Claude Opus 5.5
notes: Chapter 3 of design v4, written by Claude Opus 5.5 from plan/cards/ch03.md in the parallel wave (chapters 2–7 written at once). Draft; no audio; pictures planned only, none generated.

Story choices inside the card's beats: Gherardo's Rome tale adds a cardinal who asks him about the Cerchi (who they were, what they did, how much gold they had) and laughs at 'mercanti di lana', a small seed that the pope's side gathers information through Spini clerks. The partner who brings the news is the ch2 partner who wanted a Cerchi table in Rome (card ch2 scene 2), here unnamed (speaker char-socio-ch02). At supper Lapo repeats Bindo's «I Cerchi non congiurano: aspettano» as his own, which is what 'defends his masters too warmly' becomes. Lapo's refusal gives no principle («Non lo so. Ma non lo faccio.»), following the story bible's 'honest by default rather than by principle'. The bridge over the Arno becomes the friends' evening meeting place. The card's si vedevano was replaced by vedevamo because passive si is licensed only from G06.

Binding plant (NOTES.md): Lapo refuses to carry words for Gherardo: «Le parole, tu le senti in bottega, e la sera le porti a me... Lo fai per me?» «Non lo faccio.» Worded with portare + le parole so that ch8's «Tu non le volevi portare, ti ricordi?» recalls it exactly.

Written around later chapters' words: priori, comune (ch5) → 'Firenze li condannò'; gente, mano, notte, piazza (ch4); difendere (ch6); bere (ch7); fratello (ch5). Solo/sola (held ch8 delta) and stessi (a ch9 form of stare) avoided.

Lexicon: 47 new lexemes (ceiling 85): the 46 planned plus tirare (tira vento, da che parte tira il vento). Abaco (glossed locally once in ch1 s087) becomes a lexeme here with three uses but is dated l01, the lowest chapter that uses it (Codex review). Held deltas 8 and 15 already date the consolidated ch3 words to l03 with no card stages; their sense ids were copied. Inflected forms of ch1 and ch2 lexemes first met here are in this delta under those lexemes' ids (entry first_lesson = their chapter, forms = l03). Remoto first and second person forms (dissi, dicesti, vedesti, vedemmo) are receptive_only.

Appended to course.json bridge_references.la (COURSE.md exception; each a real Latin form with the sense used): turba, iter, fessus, quaerere, edere, narrare, exire, paene, pulcher, audire, ventus flabat, mundus, palatium, mater, nuntius, iudicium (margin glosses); dixi, dixisti, vidisti, vidimus, illos, illas, tacebat, ridebat (grammar bridge notes). Added place chunk 'San Pietro'.

Tap glosses: 71 new forms.json entries; corrected base senses that misfit (credo 'I believe' not 'to believe'; dissi, dicesti given person and tense; sei gains the numeral 'six'; lungo gains the adjective 'long'). Phrase and occurrence senses in glosses/capitolo-03.json (tavola as money-changer's table, sei 'six', da che parte tira il vento, mangiare il pane di qualcuno, lo stesso, etc.).

History: conviction of 18 April 1300 (DBI, Lapo Saltarelli) of three men tied to the Spini and the papal court, kept unnamed in the prose ('Tre uomini vicini agli Spini e al papa'); Boniface's protest of 15 May not reached: Baldo's talk is rumour. Jubilee crowd on the bridge in two streams: Dante, Inferno XVIII 28–33. Fiction (disclosed in the grammar note): Gherardo, the partner, the cardinal, Gherardo's acquaintance with the condemned.
check.mjs: 0 errors; 1 warning (continuity: this log is not yet merged into continuity.json; integration runs merge-content-deltas/finalize).

Reviews: two GPT-6.1 Sol critique rounds (prose; full apparatus) and the protocol's Codex review (gpt-6.1-sol, high): its three blockers (passive si, a copied clitic cloze, abaco dating) were fixed; suggestions taken: elided l' demonstrated, popup overrides for the key clitic lines.

Fresh-eyes review (Claude Opus): blocker fixed (Corso Donati was banished in May 1299 and at Boniface's court, so Baldo now reports him «a Roma, vicino al papa» sending word, and «Fra un anno messer Corso torna»); should-fix items applied (indicative in indirect questions against the Latin subjunctive; «L'altra sera ero un altro»; Gherardo's changed voice no longer 'tired'; same-speaker paragraphs merged; quasi and the analogical -o restated); nits applied except the caro sense and the Ser gloss (review questions).
